chapter_title: Crafting Role Components: Tasks, Handlers, Variables, and Files
chapter_summary:
Having understood the foundational concept and structure of Ansible Roles, it's time to delve into the practical aspects of building one. Each subdirectory within a role plays a crucial part in defining its behavior and functionality. Mastering these components is key to writing effective, reusable, and maintainable automation. The heart of any role lies in its `tasks/` directory, specifically the `tasks/main.yml` file. This is where you define the sequence of actions Ansible will execute when the role is applied. These tasks are identical to those you've written in regular playbooks, utilizing various modules to achieve desired states. For example, a task might install a package, create a user, or start a service. When designing tasks, always aim for idempotency – meaning running the task multiple times should result in the same system state without causing unintended side effects or errors after the first successful run. ```yaml # my_webserver_role/tasks/main.yml --- - name: Ensure Nginx package is installed ansible.builtin.package: name: nginx state: present - name: Copy Nginx configuration template ansible.builtin.template: src: nginx.conf.j2 dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf notify: Restart Nginx - name: Copy default index.html ansible.builtin.copy: src: index.html dest: /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html mode: '0644' - name: Ensure Nginx service is running and enabled ansible.builtin.service: name: nginx state: started enabled: true ``` Closely related to tasks are `handlers/`, defined in `handlers/main.yml`. Handlers are special tasks that are only triggered when explicitly `notify`'d by a task. They are typically used for actions that should only occur when a change has actually happened, such as restarting a service after its configuration file has been updated. This prevents unnecessary service restarts, which can be critical for application uptime. ```yaml # my_webserver_role/handlers/main.yml --- - name: Restart Nginx ansible.builtin.service: name: nginx state: restarted ``` In the example above, the `Copy Nginx configuration template` task will `notify: Restart Nginx` *only if* the `nginx.conf` file was actually changed. If the file was already identical, the notification would not be sent, and Nginx would not restart, preserving service continuity. Variable management is another critical aspect, primarily handled by `defaults/main.yml` and `vars/main.yml`. The distinction between these two is crucial due to Ansible's variable precedence rules. * `defaults/main.yml`: This file is for defining *default* values for variables that the role uses. Variables defined here have the *lowest precedence*. This means they can be easily overridden by variables defined in the inventory, group_vars, host_vars, `vars/main.yml` within the role, or even directly in the playbook that invokes the role. This is ideal for providing sensible, configurable options for your role, allowing consumers to customize behavior without modifying the role's core code. For example, a default Nginx port. * `vars/main.yml`: Variables defined here are specific to the role and have a *higher precedence* than `defaults/`. These are typically used for internal role variables that are not intended to be easily overridden by the role's consumer. For instance, if your role calculates a complex path or uses a temporary file name that should remain consistent internally, you'd define it here. ```yaml # my_webserver_role/defaults/main.yml --- nginx_port: 80 nginx_root_dir: /usr/share/nginx/html ``` ```yaml # my_webserver_role/vars/main.yml --- # Internal variable, not meant to be easily overridden nginx_config_path: "/etc/nginx/nginx.conf" ``` If a playbook consuming `my_webserver_role` defines `nginx_port: 8080`, it will override the default of 80. However, `nginx_config_path` from `vars/main.yml` would require a higher precedence variable (like from `host_vars` or `group_vars` with a higher priority) to be overridden. For static content, the `files/` directory is your go-to. Any file placed here can be copied directly to the managed node using the `ansible.builtin.copy` module. This is perfect for simple scripts, static HTML pages, or pre-configured binaries that don't require any dynamic adjustment. ``` # my_webserver_role/files/index.html Welcome to Cohortia Nginx!

Hello from your Cohortia Nginx server!

``` When your content needs to be dynamic, the `templates/` directory, coupled with the `ansible.builtin.template` module, becomes indispensable. Templates use Jinja2 syntax, allowing you to embed variables, loops, and conditional statements directly into your files. This is incredibly powerful for generating configuration files that adapt to different environments or host-specific settings. ```jinja2 # my_webserver_role/templates/nginx.conf.j2 user nginx; worker_processes auto; error_log /var/log/nginx/error.log warn; pid /var/run/nginx.pid; events { worker_connections 1024; } http { include /etc/nginx/mime.types; default_type application/octet-stream; log_format main '$remote_addr - $remote_user [$time_local] "$request" ' '$status $body_bytes_sent "$http_referer" ' '"$http_user_agent" "$http_x_forwarded_for"'; access_log /var/log/nginx/access.log main; sendfile on; #tcp_nopush on; keepalive_timeout 65; #gzip on; server { listen {{ nginx_port }}; # Using a variable from defaults/ server_name localhost; location / { root {{ nginx_root_dir }}; # Using a variable from defaults/ index index.html index.htm; } error_page 500 502 503 504 /50x.html; location = /50x.html { root /usr/share/nginx/html; } } } ``` Notice how `{{ nginx_port }}` and `{{ nginx_root_dir }}` are used in the template. These will be replaced by the values defined in `defaults/main.yml` (or overridden elsewhere) when Ansible renders the template. A common mistake is confusing `files/` and `templates/`. If you try to use `ansible.builtin.copy` with a Jinja2 template, it will copy the template verbatim without rendering the variables, leading to a non-functional configuration. Conversely, using `ansible.builtin.template` with a plain file from `files/` will attempt to parse it as Jinja2, which might fail or produce unexpected results if the file contains Jinja2-like syntax that isn't intended to be processed. Always ensure you use the correct module for the type of content you're deploying. Another frequent error is mismanaging variable precedence, leading to unexpected values being used. Always remember `defaults/` are easily overridden, while `vars/` are more persistent within the role. By carefully structuring your tasks, handlers, variables, and content files within their respective directories, you build a robust and flexible role that can be easily understood, maintained, and reused across various automation scenarios. This modular approach is fundamental to becoming proficient in Ansible automation.

screens.title: Crafting Role Components
screens.subtitle: Tasks, Handlers, Variables, and Files for a reusable Ansible role

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how the pieces of an Ansible role fit together so you can build reliable, reusable automation. We will focus on the role directories you use every day: tasks and handlers that drive changes, defaults and vars that manage configuration and precedence, and files versus templates for static and dynamic content. You will see concrete examples of a my_webserver_role that installs Nginx, deploys a static index page, and renders a configuration file using Jinja2. Understanding these parts matters because well-structured roles make it safe to share automation across teams and avoid surprise behavior when variables are overridden. A common misconception is that all role variables are equally easy to change; we'll show how defaults are intentionally low precedence and vars are higher and therefore used for role-internal values. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to assemble a role, choose the right directory for each asset, and link a notification from a template task to a handler so services only restart when necessary.

keyIdea.title: What you'll master
keyIdea.text: Assemble role components so tasks drive change, handlers react only after real changes, variables are organized by precedence, and files/templates are used correctly for static or dynamic content.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify where task logic lives in a role and how handlers respond only after changes. You'll differentiate between defaults and vars based on variable precedence and intent, and you will choose the correct directory for static files versus templates that require Jinja2 rendering. Each objective maps to practical actions: reading or authoring tasks/main. yml and handlers/main. yml, placing reusable defaults in defaults/main. yml, reserving vars/main. yml for role-internal values, and placing content either in files/ for straight copy or templates/ for rendered configuration. For example, you'll practice writing a template that uses nginx_port from defaults and use notify to trigger a handler only when the rendered config changes. A common misconception is treating defaults as immutable; instead, they are deliberately low precedence so that the consumer of your role can tailor behavior without changing the role itself. These objectives help you create roles that are predictable, testable, and safe to share.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Why They Matter
screens.subtitle: Practical outcomes and common confusions resolved

narration.text: These objectives are hands-on. You won't just name directories; you'll use them correctly. For tasks, you will author steps that are idempotent so running a playbook twice does not break a system. For handlers, you'll link notify statements so expensive operations like service restarts occur only when needed. For variables, you'll practice placing tunable defaults in defaults/main. yml so consumers can override them, and keep role internals in vars/main. yml so they remain consistent. For files and templates, you'll deploy a static index. html via the copy module and render a configuration using the template module with Jinja2 variables. A frequent mistake to watch for is treating a Jinja2 file in files/ as if it will render; copy will not substitute variables. Another is placing a configurable option in vars/main. yml expecting easy overrides. These exercises make sure that when you share a role, it behaves predictably and is easy for others to customize.

keyIdea.title: Practical focus
keyIdea.text: Build idempotent tasks, notify handlers correctly, and place variables and content where they behave as intended when roles are reused.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Learning Objectives
Why idempotency matters

Idempotent tasks reduce risk in automation by ensuring multiple runs do not change a system unexpectedly. Practice ensures safer rollouts and simpler debugging.

Why variable precedence matters

Correct precedence prevents surprise values. Defaults are intentionally low precedence so operators can override behavior without editing the role.

Why choosing files or templates matters

Using template for configuration that needs variables ensures the final file is tailored to the host; using copy for static files avoids unnecessary template processing.

VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

By completing the chapter exercises you will demonstrate each of these skills in a deployable my_webserver_role.

screens.title: Role Tasks: tasks/main.yml
screens.subtitle: The sequence of operations that make a role do work

narration.text: A role's tasks directory, and especially tasks/main. yml, is the heart of the role. It contains the ordered list of operations Ansible runs when the role is applied. Each entry is a standard Ansible task using modules like package, copy, template, or service. The crucial property to aim for is idempotency: a task should leave the system in the same state if run multiple times. For example, installing a package with state: present will ensure the package exists without re-installing unnecessarily. In the provided Nginx role example you will see tasks to install Nginx, template the configuration, copy a static index. html, and ensure the service is started and enabled. A concrete example is the copy of index. html which deploys a static page; because copy checks checksums, it only updates the file when content differs. A common misconception is that tasks must be minimal; instead, tasks should be clearly named and grouped to make failure points obvious. Key takeaway: author tasks as clear, idempotent steps with meaningful names so the role is maintainable and predictable. How will you structure your tasks to make error diagnosis straightforward?

keyIdea.title: Tasks drive the role
keyIdea.text: tasks/main.yml lists the steps Ansible executes. Make each task idempotent and descriptive so playbook runs are predictable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Role Tasks
Definition

Tasks are the ordered actions executed by a role. They use modules and should be idempotent so repeated runs do not produce unintended changes.

Common patterns
  • Install packages with state: present
  • Deploy configuration files using template or copy
  • Ensure services are started and enabled
Key Takeaway

Name tasks clearly and keep them idempotent. That makes role runs repeatable and easier to debug.

Example: tasks/main.yml
# my_webserver_role/tasks/main.yml
---
- name: Ensure Nginx package is installed
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: nginx
    state: present

- name: Copy Nginx configuration template
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: nginx.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
  notify: Restart Nginx

- name: Copy default index.html
  ansible.builtin.copy:
    src: index.html
    dest: /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
    mode: '0644'

- name: Ensure Nginx service is running and enabled
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: started
    enabled: true
Common mistake

Grouping unrelated changes into one task can hide failures. Keep tasks focused and idempotent.

screens.title: Handlers and notify: React only on real change
screens.subtitle: Use handlers to perform conditional actions like service restarts

narration.text: Handlers are special tasks kept in handlers/main. yml that run only when another task in the play triggers a notify. They are useful for operations that should happen after a change, such as restarting a service after updating its configuration. The mechanism is simple: a task that changes state includes a notify: Handler Name line. If the task made a change, Ansible queues the handler and runs handlers at the end of the play for that host. If nothing changed, the handler is not run. A concrete example is templating nginx. conf and notifying Restart Nginx. If the template content is identical to the existing file, the template task reports no change and the handler does not run, preventing unnecessary restarts and preserving uptime. A frequent misconception is assuming notify triggers instantaneous execution; it does not — handlers run after task execution for efficiency and to consolidate duplicates. Design handlers to be idempotent too and name them clearly so they match the notify text exactly. How will you use handlers to minimize service disruptions in your roles? Handlers and notify: React only on real change means handlers run only when notified by changed tasks. use them for restart or reload operations to avoid unnecessary work.. In practical terms, use handlers to perform conditional actions like service restarts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Handlers defer conditional actions
keyIdea.text: Handlers run only when notified by changed tasks. Use them for restart or reload operations to avoid unnecessary work.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Handlers & notify
How handlers work
  1. A task runs and reports whether it changed the system.
  2. If the task has notify and changed, the handler is queued for that host.
  3. Handlers run after tasks complete for the host, once per unique handler name.
Pro tip

Name handlers clearly and keep their actions minimal so rollbacks and debugging remain simple.

Example: handlers/main.yml
# my_webserver_role/handlers/main.yml
---
- name: Restart Nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: restarted
Key Takeaway

Handlers let you defer and consolidate actions such as restarts. They only run if a notifier reports a change.

screens.title: defaults/main.yml — Role defaults
screens.subtitle: Low-precedence variables meant to be easily overridden

narration.text: defaults/main. yml is where you place sensible default values for a role. These variables have the lowest precedence among role-level variable files, which makes them the preferred place for options you expect consumers to override. For example, defining nginx_port: 80 and nginx_root_dir: /usr/share/nginx/html in defaults gives the role usable behavior out of the box while allowing inventory, group_vars, host_vars, or a playbook to override those defaults. This behavior matters because it enables role reuse without editing role code. A common misstep is putting tunable options into vars/main. yml and then being surprised when operators can't override them as easily. Remember: defaults are intentionally permissive. When you choose variable names, document them and provide reasonable values so others can adopt your role with minimal changes. Example: override nginx_port in a playbook to run a test instance on a non-standard port. How will you document defaults in your roles so users know what can be changed? defaults/main.yml — Role defaults means put user-facing options in defaults/main.yml. these values are easy to override from outside the role.. In practical terms, low-precedence variables meant to be easily overridden. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Defaults are overridable
keyIdea.text: Put user-facing options in defaults/main.yml. These values are easy to override from outside the role.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › defaults/main.yml
Role defaults explained

Defaults provide sensible base values for role behavior. Because they are low precedence, they are intended to be easily overridden by the role consumer.

When to use defaults
  • Ports, directory paths, and other configuration options meant to be tuned
  • Values that make the role turnkey but editable
Example override

A playbook can set nginx_port: 8080 to override the default of 80, letting you run a testing instance without changing the role.

Example: defaults/main.yml
# my_webserver_role/defaults/main.yml
---
nginx_port: 80
nginx_root_dir: /usr/share/nginx/html
Mnemonic

Defaults are the friendly, overridable layer — think 'user-configurable starting points'.

screens.title: vars/main.yml — Role internal variables
screens.subtitle: Use vars for role-internal values with higher precedence

narration.text: vars/main. yml holds variables intended to be internal to the role and to have higher precedence than defaults. Use this file when a value is part of the role's internal logic and should not be easily overridden by an end user. For instance, nginx_config_path: "/etc/nginx/nginx. conf" is an internal pointer used by tasks and handlers. Because vars have a higher precedence than defaults, placing a configurable option mistakenly in vars makes it harder for users to change from outside. A concrete example: if you put nginx_port in vars, a playbook-level override will typically still win, but certain other variable sources may not. The practical rule is: defaults for options you expect consumers to tune; vars for constants or calculated internals that must remain consistent. A common misconception is that vars are private in a strict sense; they are not sealed from override, but they are intentionally higher precedence so the role's internals remain stable. Reflect: which of your role values should be easily overridden, and which should stay constant? vars/main.yml — Role internal variables means place role-internal constants or calculated paths in vars/main.yml so they remain consistent across runs.. In practical terms, use vars for role-internal values with higher precedence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Vars are for internals
keyIdea.text: Place role-internal constants or calculated paths in vars/main.yml so they remain consistent across runs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › vars/main.yml
Role internals

Use vars/main.yml for variables that should remain consistent and are part of role implementation details rather than user-facing options.

When to prefer vars
  • Paths or names that the role's tasks rely on
  • Calculated values used by multiple internal tasks
Example: vars/main.yml
# my_webserver_role/vars/main.yml
---
# Internal variable, not meant to be easily overridden
nginx_config_path: "/etc/nginx/nginx.conf"
Contrast

defaults: user-friendly and overridable. vars: role-internal and higher precedence.

screens.title: files/ — Static content with copy
screens.subtitle: Place verbatim files here and deploy with the copy module

narration.text: The files/ directory is for static assets that should be copied verbatim to managed nodes using the ansible. builtin. copy module. Typical uses include scripts, static H T M L, or prebuilt binaries that do not need rendering. A concrete example from the chapter is index. html placed in files and deployed unchanged. Because copy transfers the file as-is, it preserves content and permissions but will not process any Jinja2 expressions. A common mistake is placing a Jinja2 template in files and expecting variables to be substituted; this will result in an unrendered file on the target. Use files/ when content is identical for every host, and use the copy module in tasks to deploy it. The key takeaway is to match the asset type to the correct directory and module: static assets go to files/ with copy, dynamic assets go to templates/ with template. How will you check whether an asset needs rendering before placing it in files/ or templates/? files/ — Static content with copy means use files/ for static content and deploy it with ansible.builtin.copy so it is copied without rendering.. In practical terms, place verbatim files here and deploy with the copy module. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: files is for verbatim assets
keyIdea.text: Use files/ for static content and deploy it with ansible.builtin.copy so it is copied without rendering.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › files/ directory
When to use files/

Put assets that do not require variable substitution, like plain HTML pages, scripts, or binaries, in files/ and use the copy module to deploy them.

Common mistake

Expecting Jinja2 to render inside files/. The copy module will not process templates.

Example: files/index.html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Welcome to Cohortia Nginx!</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Hello from your Cohortia Nginx server!</h1>
</body>
</html>
Key Takeaway

If a file should be copied exactly as authored, place it in files/ and use ansible.builtin.copy.

screens.title: templates/ — Jinja2 for dynamic configuration
screens.subtitle: Render variables, conditionals, and loops for per-host configs

narration.text: Templates live in templates/ and are processed by the ansible. builtin. template module using Jinja2 syntax. Templates let you inject variables, run loops, and evaluate conditionals so configuration files adapt to host-specific values. The chapter's nginx. conf. j2 example demonstrates using {{ nginx_port }} and {{ nginx_root_dir }} so the same template renders differently depending on variable values supplied from defaults, inventory, or playbooks. A useful behavior is that template will only mark a change if the rendered content differs from the target file on the host, which means handlers notified by the template task will run only when the configuration actually changes. A common error is putting Jinja2 into files/ and using copy; variables will not be substituted. When authoring templates, keep logic readable, avoid complex Python inside templates, and prefer small, documented variables. Example: a template sets server listen to the nginx_port default while an operator can override that value in a playbook for testing. Closing question: what variables will you expose in defaults so your templates remain flexible yet safe? templates/ — Jinja2 for dynamic configuration means put jinja2 files in templates/ and use the template module to render host-specific configuration before copying to the node.. In practical terms, render variables, conditionals, and loops for per-host configs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Templates are rendered
keyIdea.text: Put Jinja2 files in templates/ and use the template module to render host-specific configuration before copying to the node.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › templates/ directory
Why templates

Templates allow files to be generated with variables and logic, so a single template can serve multiple environments or hosts.

Design tips
  • Keep templates readable and well-documented
  • Avoid deep logic; prefer precomputed variables in vars or tasks
Example: nginx.conf.j2
# my_webserver_role/templates/nginx.conf.j2
user  nginx;
worker_processes  auto;

error_log  /var/log/nginx/error.log warn;
pid        /var/run/nginx.pid;

events {
    worker_connections  1024;
}

http {
    include       /etc/nginx/mime.types;
    default_type  application/octet-stream;

    server {
        listen       {{ nginx_port }}; # Using a variable from defaults/
        server_name  localhost;

        location / {
            root   {{ nginx_root_dir }}; # Using a variable from defaults/
            index  index.html index.htm;
        }
    }
}
Key Takeaway

Templates let you produce per-host files from a single source, keeping roles flexible and maintainable.

screens.title: Copy vs Template modules
screens.subtitle: Choose the right module to match the file type

narration.text: Choosing between the copy and template modules is a common decision when building roles. Use copy when you want to transfer a file verbatim from files/ to the managed node. Use template when the file needs variable substitution or Jinja2 logic and lives in templates/. The practical difference is that template renders Jinja2 expressions and only reports a change when the rendered output differs; copy transfers the file content and reports change when checksums differ. A concrete example: index. html should usually be in files/ and deployed with copy, while nginx. conf with {{ nginx_port }} belongs in templates/ and is rendered. A frequent mistake is placing a template in files/ and expecting variables to be substituted — the result will be an unrendered template on the node. Another problem is using template for binary files; template is meant for text files and may corrupt binaries. Key takeaway: match file type and intent to the correct directory and module to avoid silent failures. What checks will you add to CI to catch incorrect module choices? Copy vs Template modules means copy = verbatim deploy from files/. template = render jinja2 from templates/ before copying.. In practical terms, choose the right module to match the file type. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Match intent to module
keyIdea.text: copy = verbatim deploy from files/. template = render Jinja2 from templates/ before copying.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Copy vs Template
Copy (files/)
  • Use for static text files, scripts, and binaries (no rendering)
  • Deployed with ansible.builtin.copy
Mistake to avoid

Putting a Jinja2 template in files/ and expecting rendering.

Template (templates/)
  • Use for dynamic configuration that requires variables or conditionals
  • Deployed with ansible.builtin.template and rendered via Jinja2
Pro tip

Keep template logic small; compute complex values in tasks or vars to keep templates readable.

Quick checks
If you need variables or conditionals, put the file in templates/ and use template. If the file is identical for all hosts, use files/ and copy.

screens.title: Assembling the role: from defaults to tasks
screens.subtitle: Integrate defaults, vars, templates and handlers into a working role

narration.text: Putting the pieces together makes a role useful. Start by defining sensible defaults in defaults/main. yml such as nginx_port and nginx_root_dir. Add any role-internal constants in vars/main. yml like nginx_config_path. Place static assets such as index. html in files/ and dynamic configs such as nginx. conf. j2 in templates/. Then write tasks/main. yml to install Nginx, deploy the template and static file, and ensure the service is running. Finally, add handlers/main. yml with a Restart Nginx handler and notify it from the template task. A concrete playbook to run the role looks like deploy_nginx. yml which lists the role under roles:. Run ansible-playbook deploy_nginx. yml against your inventory and verify the site. A useful pattern when assembling roles is to test variables by overriding defaults in a simple playbook and running the role locally so you can quickly confirm template rendering and handler behavior. Common misconception: assembling pieces in any order will work; in practice, define variables before tasks reference them and keep templates consistent with variable names. Takeaway: follow a clear order and test each piece in isolation before integrating.

keyIdea.title: Assemble & test iteratively
keyIdea.text: Define defaults and vars, add files and templates, implement tasks and handlers, then test the role with a playbook to confirm behavior.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Assembling the role
Step-by-step
  1. Create defaults/main.yml for tunable options.
  2. Add templates/nginx.conf.j2 and files/index.html.
  3. Write tasks/main.yml to install package, template config, copy file, and start service.
  4. Define handlers/main.yml and notify from template task.
  5. Test with a small playbook and inspect rendered files on the host.
Example playbook: deploy_nginx.yml
# deploy_nginx.yml
---
- name: Deploy Nginx web server using a role
  hosts: your_target_server
  become: true
  roles:
    - my_webserver_role
Key Takeaway

Integrate pieces in order and validate by running the role; confirm templates render and handlers only execute after real changes.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: How to diagnose template, variable, and handler issues

narration.text: When building roles you will run into a small set of recurring problems. First, incorrect placement of Jinja2 — putting it in files/ instead of templates/ — leads to unrendered content on the managed host. You can diagnose this by opening the deployed file and looking for raw template markers such as double curly braces. Second, variable precedence confusion: when a setting doesn't change as expected, inspect where the variable is defined. Remember defaults are low precedence and intended to be overridden; vars are higher and intended for internals. Use debug tasks to print variable sources during a play to confirm which value wins. Third, unexpected handler behavior often comes from assuming notify triggers immediate action. Handlers run after tasks and are queued per host; duplicate notifications will consolidate into a single handler run. When a handler doesn't run, confirm the notifying task actually reported changed: modules like template and copy will indicate change only when the target differs. Practical checks: run the playbook with -v to see task changed statuses, inspect the rendered file on the host, and add a temporary debug: var={{ nginx_port }} task to verify values. Ending question: which of these checks will you include in your role's CI pipeline to catch regressions early?

keyIdea.title: Diagnose with change and debug
keyIdea.text: When things go wrong, check whether tasks reported changed, inspect rendered files, and print variables to find source and precedence issues.

content.html:
Troubleshoot › Chapter 5.2 › Common mistakes
Frequent issues
  • Jinja2 in files/ leading to unrendered templates on nodes.
  • Placing user-tunable options in vars/main.yml making them hard to override.
  • Assuming handlers run immediately; they run after tasks and only if a change occurred.
Quick diagnostics

Run the playbook with -v, inspect the changed status, view the target file, and add debug tasks to print variables.

Example debug task
- name: Debug nginx_port
  ansible.builtin.debug:
    var: nginx_port
Check

If the value printed isn't what you expect, inspect inventory, group_vars, host_vars, and role vars to find the source.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders from this chapter

narration.text: Remember these concise points as you build roles. First, tasks in tasks/main. yml are the procedural heart of a role; write them idempotently and name them clearly so runs are predictable and failures easy to trace. Second, handlers live in handlers/main. yml and run only when a notifying task reports a change; use them for restarts or reloads to avoid unnecessary disruptions. Third, defaults/main. yml and vars/main. yml differ in precedence and intent: defaults are low-precedence, consumer-overridable settings; vars are higher-precedence, role-internal variables. Carry these principles into your role design and you will produce automation that is safe to reuse and simple to customize. narration.text: A final set of reminders: use files/ with ansible. builtin. copy for static assets and templates/ with ansible. builtin. template for dynamic files rendered with Jinja2. When you need to restart services, prefer handlers triggered by notify rather than restarting unconditionally inside tasks. And finally, test roles by overriding defaults in a simple playbook and running the playbook twice to observe idempotency and handler behavior. These practices prevent common surprises and make roles easier to share and maintain.
